Baby & Child

Duplex kidneys in children: duplicated ureters and care

Updated: November 10, 2026

Written and edited by BeMama Authors team: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

A scan report that mentions a duplex kidney can sound alarming. It describes how part of the urinary drainage system formed before birth, and many children with this finding stay well without treatment. The useful next question is whether urine flows freely and the kidney tissue works well. The name alone does not tell you that an operation is needed.

What does a duplex kidney mean?

A kidney normally collects urine into a drainage area called the renal pelvis, then sends it through a tube called the ureter to the bladder. In a duplex kidney, there are two collecting areas within the kidney, often described as upper and lower parts or moieties. Each has its own drainage route. This is usually a difference within one kidney, rather than an entirely separate third kidney.

The variation may affect the right kidney, the left kidney or both. The ureter is different from the urethra, which carries urine from the bladder out of the body. Understanding those names helps make a scan report clearer. A duplex collecting system is also different from polycystic kidney disease, a missing kidney or a multicystic dysplastic kidney, although other developmental differences can sometimes coexist.

Complete and incomplete duplication

With incomplete, or partial, duplication, two drainage tubes leave the kidney and join before reaching the bladder, forming a Y-shaped route. With complete duplication, the tubes remain separate. Their openings and the way urine drains are important: one tube can enter in an unusual position, rather than both connecting normally to the bladder.

A report may describe a duplicated pelvicalyceal system or two renal pelves. Ask the clinician to explain whether only the collecting areas are doubled, whether there are two ureters, and whether their full course is clear. The term complete does not by itself measure kidney damage. Decisions depend on drainage, infections and the function of each part, not simply the label.

How common is it, and why does it happen?

Duplex kidneys are a relatively common urinary-tract variation, often estimated to affect around one person in a hundred. Exact estimates differ because many people have no symptoms and never need a scan. Partial duplication is more common than complete duplication. Girls are affected more often, but boys can have the same anatomy and may also need assessment if symptoms develop.

The difference arises while the collecting system and ureters develop before birth. There is no evidence that a parent’s ordinary actions or omissions during pregnancy caused it. It can run in families, but the genetic explanation is not always known. A general inheritance percentage cannot reliably predict an individual family’s risk; share relevant family history and ask whether any further family assessment would be useful.

Many children have no symptoms

When the collecting areas drain properly, a child may have no discomfort, urinary problems or loss of kidney function. The finding can be discovered by chance during pregnancy, after a urinary infection or on a scan done for another reason. Having an extra drainage tube does not automatically mean the child produces more urine or has a dangerous kidney disease.

The duplicated anatomy does not ordinarily disappear as the child grows. What may improve is an associated problem, such as some forms of urinary reflux. A plan for observation means that treatment is unnecessary at present, not that the extra tube must dissolve. Conversely, pain should not be dismissed because the original scan finding was described as harmless: infection, blockage or another cause may need attention.

Problems with drainage, reflux and ureteroceles

A ureterocele is a balloon-like enlargement near the end of a ureter, usually where it enters the bladder. It can narrow or obstruct drainage. Urine then backs up and stretches the collecting system, a finding called hydronephrosis; the ureter may widen too. The amount of swelling and its effect on function vary. Swelling on a scan is a finding to investigate, not proof that the whole kidney has stopped working.

Vesicoureteral reflux means urine travels backward from the bladder toward a kidney. An unusual ureter opening can allow this to happen. Reflux and poor drainage can increase the risk of urinary infection, and some children develop kidney scars. Low-grade reflux may improve, but severity alone does not determine treatment: infections, bladder function, kidney findings and the child’s age also matter. Do not wait for repeated infections before following up a concerning result.

Ectopic ureters and persistent wetting

An ectopic ureter ends in an unusual location, sometimes outside the bladder. In a girl, an opening below the muscle that holds urine in can cause continuous dribbling even though she also passes urine normally on the toilet. Persistently damp underwear after toilet training deserves assessment. This pattern differs from occasional accidents, but wetting alone cannot establish the diagnosis.

Boys usually do not have the same constant-dribbling pattern because the abnormal opening is generally above that control muscle. They may instead develop urinary infections or, less commonly, inflammation around the tube behind a testicle. Never assume new scrotal pain is explained by a known duplex kidney. Sudden severe testicular pain, or pain with vomiting or abdominal pain, requires emergency assessment because twisting of the testicle is another possible cause.

Symptoms that need medical help

Arrange prompt assessment for fever, painful urination, new frequent urination, blood in urine, abdominal or back pain, or repeated wetting after a period of dryness. Babies with a urinary infection may mainly have fever, poor feeding, vomiting or unusual irritability. With a known urinary-tract abnormality, fever suggesting a urinary infection needs urgent same-day medical advice; the child may need hospital assessment. Tell the clinician about the duplex system and any preventive antibiotics.

Get emergency help for severe illness, difficulty breathing, collapse, unusual difficulty waking, or inability to pass urine with a painful swollen lower abdomen. Severe side pain or repeated vomiting that prevents drinking also needs urgent assessment. A baby under three months with a temperature of 38°C or higher needs immediate medical assessment. Do not wait for a routine scan appointment, a higher temperature or every symptom to appear.

What scans and tests can show

Ultrasound is commonly the first investigation. Before birth it may suggest duplication or swelling; after birth it can assess the kidneys, drainage areas and bladder. The timing of a baby’s follow-up scan depends on the prenatal findings and symptoms. Ask for a clear plan before leaving maternity care. Not every child requires every imaging test, and a simple scan cannot answer every question about reflux or how each kidney segment works.

If further detail is needed, a VCUG, also called an MCUG, uses a small bladder catheter and imaging during filling and urination to look for reflux. Nuclear-medicine scans such as DMSA or MAG3 can answer selected questions about kidney tissue, relative function or drainage. MR urography can help clarify complex anatomy. The team should explain the purpose and any radiation or sedation considerations. Urine testing checks for infection; blood tests may assess overall kidney function.

Observation and antibiotics

If the child is well and assessment shows uncomplicated drainage, no operation or medicine may be needed. Some children can leave specialist follow-up after reassuring checks; others need further scans or appointments. Confirm which applies and which symptoms should trigger contact. Keeping the reports and follow-up plan helps other clinicians understand the anatomy without assuming that every future illness is caused by it.

An active bacterial urinary infection is treated with prescribed antibiotics. Some children with particular drainage problems or reflux are also offered a lower-dose preventive antibiotic. That is a separate decision, balancing the risk of infection against adverse effects and antibiotic resistance. It is not needed for every duplex kidney. Follow the prescription and contact the team about illness even while preventive treatment is being taken; do not start leftover medicine or change the dose yourself.

When surgery may be considered

An operation may be recommended for significant obstruction, persistent leakage from an ectopic ureter, recurrent infections or a poorly functioning segment causing problems. Options include opening an obstructing ureterocele, joining one ureter to the other, or moving a ureter’s insertion into the bladder. Removing a poorly functioning part of a kidney is considered in selected circumstances; removing an entire kidney is not the automatic response to duplication.

The surgeon weighs the function worth preserving, the position of the tubes, reflux, bladder emptying and the child’s overall condition. An infected obstructed system can require urgent drainage rather than waiting for a planned reconstruction. Sometimes more than one procedure is needed. Ask what the proposed operation aims to fix, what alternatives exist, and what follow-up, wound care, medicines and activity advice will be needed afterward.

Daily life and the next appointment

Most children with an uncomplicated duplex kidney can play, attend nursery or school and take part in ordinary activities. The finding alone is not a reason to impose a restrictive kidney diet or stop sport. If kidney function is reduced, symptoms are ongoing or surgery has just taken place, follow the child’s individual plan. Sensible toilet routines and treatment of constipation may help associated bladder problems, but they do not change the duplicated anatomy.

Ask the team: Which side and which part are affected? Is there reflux, obstruction, a ureterocele or an ectopic opening? How well does each part work? Is another test needed, and what would its result change? Know whom to contact for fever or urinary symptoms. If wetting is affecting the child’s confidence, offer practical support without blame; persistent leakage is a medical concern, not evidence that the child is being careless.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Ask for an explanation of the anatomy, drainage and kidney-function findings, rather than relying on the scan label alone.

Keep the follow-up plan and know how to get urgent help for fever or urinary symptoms.

Discuss benefits, risks and alternatives before starting preventive antibiotics or arranging surgery.

How BeMama can help

BeMama can help organize scan appointments, symptoms and questions for the care team. It cannot interpret urinary imaging, diagnose infection or decide whether a child needs surgery.

When to seek help

Seek prompt assessment for urinary symptoms or fever in a child with a known urinary-tract abnormality. Severe illness, difficulty breathing, collapse, unusual difficulty waking or sudden severe testicular pain needs emergency help. Do not change prescribed antibiotics without advice.

Evidence notes updated: November 10, 2026

Key takeaways

  • A duplex kidney describes a duplicated collecting system; many children need no treatment.
  • Complete and incomplete duplication describe anatomy, not the degree of kidney damage.
  • The extra drainage route persists, while some associated problems may improve with growth.
  • Infections, obstruction, reflux or continuous leakage guide testing and treatment choices.
  • Fever or urinary symptoms need prompt assessment, especially with a known urinary-tract abnormality.

Frequently asked questions

Is a duplex kidney painful?

Often it causes no pain. However, infection, obstruction or another condition can cause abdominal, back or urinary pain. New pain should be assessed rather than dismissed because the child’s duplicated system was previously uncomplicated.

What causes it, and is it inherited?

It develops before birth as the kidney’s collecting areas and ureters form. It can run in families, but the exact genetic mechanism is not always known. The finding is not evidence that a parent caused it during pregnancy. Ask for advice based on your family history instead of relying on a universal inheritance percentage.

Is it more common in girls or boys?

It is more common in girls, but boys can also have a duplex collecting system. Sex does not decide whether treatment is needed; drainage, kidney function and any symptoms matter.

What is the difference between complete and incomplete duplication?

In incomplete duplication, two ureters join before reaching the bladder. In complete duplication they remain separate, and one may end in an unusual place. Either form needs to be understood alongside the child’s scan findings and symptoms.

Will my child grow out of the extra ureter?

The duplicated drainage anatomy ordinarily remains. Some associated reflux may improve as a child grows. No treatment being needed is different from the anatomical duplication disappearing.

Does a duplex kidney always need surgery?

No. Many children remain well without surgery. An operation is considered when a specific complication, such as obstruction, recurrent infection or persistent ectopic-ureter leakage, warrants correction. The team aims to preserve useful kidney tissue where possible.

Can continuous wetting be related?

Yes. In girls, an ectopic ureter below the urine-control muscle can cause persistent dribbling despite normal toilet use. Other causes of wetting are also possible. Arrange assessment and avoid blaming the child or assuming more toilet training will resolve the problem.

Should we wait for the next scan if our child develops fever?

No. Seek urgent same-day medical advice for possible urinary infection and explain the known urinary anatomy. A baby under three months with a temperature of 38°C or higher needs immediate assessment. Severe illness, breathing difficulty, collapse or unusual difficulty waking requires emergency help.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
